entry.title: 2514819 (Refugee) [2026] ARTA 2331
entry.content:
The applicant, an Indonesian woman, sought protection claiming political activism and membership/support of the Islamic Defenders’ Front (FPI), plus a 7 December 2020 attack. The Tribunal accepted the attack occurred but rejected the FPI and political claims as not credible. It affirmed the delegate’s refusal, finding no real chance of serious harm or real risk of significant harm on return to Indonesia.

Key holding: A protection claim may fail where the applicant’s core new claim is late-disclosed, insufficiently detailed, and inconsistent with country information, even if a separate incident of harm is accepted.

I consider the late disclosure, the lack of sufficient details, and the inconsistency with country information to be most pertinent in establishing the credibility of the applicant's claim, and overall I am not satisfied the applicant was a member of the FPI, or that she had a [business] that provided services to the FPI.

Administrative Review Tribunal, 16 Jul 2026, [2026] ARTA 2331

entry.title: 2407106 (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2270
entry.content:
The Tribunal reviewed a delegate’s refusal of a Student (Temporary) (Class TU) visa because a bogus bank document had supported the applicant’s earlier Temporary Activity visa. The Tribunal accepted the document was bogus but found the applicant was unaware of it and neither complicit in nor recklessly indifferent to her coach’s or agent’s conduct. It set aside the refusal and remitted the matter with a direction that PIC 4020 is met for cl 500.217(1).

Key holding: For PIC 4020(1), where a third party supplies a bogus document, an applicant may be taken to have caused it to be given if complicit in, or recklessly indifferent to, that third party’s unlawful or dishonest conduct.

If the applicant is complicit in the provision of false information or 'indifferent' to a third party acting unlawfully or dishonestly, it can be said that the applicant caused it to be given.

Administrative Review Tribunal, 1 Jul 2026, [2026] ARTA 2270

entry.title: The Owners - Strata Plan No 87231 v 3A Composites GmbH (No 10) [2026] FCA 351 (27 March 2026)
entry.content:
A consumer class action brought by strata corporations against the German manufacturer (3A Composites) and Australian distributor (Halifax Vogel Group) of Alucobond PE and Alucobond Plus aluminium composite panel (ACP) cladding products, alleging the products were not of acceptable/merchantable quality and that marketing materials were misleading. The claims failed on both grounds after a lengthy trial before Anderson J in the Federal Court.

entry.title: 1906822 (Refugee) [2024] AATA 4181
entry.content:
The applicant, an Indian national from Tamil Nadu, sought protection alleging Q Branch police would harm him because he knew of their alleged drug trafficking and sexual abuse involving Sri Lankan Tamil refugee workers. The Tribunal affirmed the delegate’s refusal, finding the applicant’s claims and evidence lacked credibility and reliability. This is a fact-and-credibility-based protection visa review.

Administrative Review Tribunal, 11 Oct 2024, [2024] AATA 4181

entry.title: Brar (Migration) [2024] AATA 4014
entry.content:
The Tribunal reviewed the consequential cancellation of Mr Brar’s Subclass 309 partner visa after his sponsor wife’s Subclass 119 visa was cancelled for incorrect information and bogus documents. Although the Tribunal accepted Mr Brar may not have known of his wife’s fraud, it affirmed the cancellation after weighing his child-custody and hardship claims.

entry.title: 2112075 (Refugee) [2024] AATA 4284
entry.content:
This was a review of a delegate’s refusal of a protection visa to an applicant whose country of reference was Kiribati. The applicant originally claimed a [Country 1] identity and a land-dispute fear, but later said he was born in [Country 4] to Kiribati parents, was fostered in [Country 1], and had obtained a [Country 1] passport using false identity details. The Tribunal affirmed the refusal, including because a bogus document had been provided without reasonable explanation.

Key holding: Where an applicant has provided a bogus document as evidence of identity, nationality or citizenship without a reasonable explanation, the grant of a protection visa is prevented in any case.

bogus document provided as evidence of identity, nationality or citizenship - no reasonable explanation - grant of visa prevented in any case - decision under review affirmed

entry.title: 1907161 (Refugee) [2024] AATA 4231
entry.content:
The Tribunal reviewed a refusal of a protection visa to an Indian national Sikh who claimed to fear his former employer [Mr A], Indian police/NCB, and harm as a Sikh and through relatives linked to Sikh separatism. The Tribunal rejected the claims as not credible or not supported by country information and affirmed the refusal. It found the applicant did not meet either the refugee or complementary protection criteria.

entry.title: SRFX and Minister for Immigration, Citizenship and Multicultural Affairs (Citizenship) [2024] AATA 3549
entry.content:
SRFX applied for Australian citizenship by conferral, but a delegate refused approval under s 24(1) of the Australian Citizenship Act 2007 (Cth), finding he did not satisfy the good character requirement in s 21(2)(h) and that his identity could not be established under s 24(3). The Tribunal reviewed the decision, relying on the applicant’s migration history, prior partner visa findings and allegedly bogus documents, and affirmed the refusal. The case turns on whether the Tribunal could be satisfied of his good character and identity.

Key holding: In assessing good character for citizenship, the decision-maker must make a holistic assessment of the person’s enduring moral qualities, and a single sufficiently serious adverse incident can outweigh otherwise good qualities.

The decision-maker must look holistically at applicant's behaviour over time and reach a conclusion about the person's enduring moral qualities. Notwithstanding the obligation to take a holistic approach, it is established that a single adverse incident of sufficient weight and seriousness can outweigh many good qualities in a person.

Administrative Review Tribunal, 8 Oct 2024, [2024] AATA 3549

entry.title: 2009058 (Refugee) [2024] AATA 4435
entry.content:
The Tribunal affirmed the refusal of a protection visa to a Thai applicant who claimed Red Shirt political activism, past arrest/questioning, and fear of arrest or killing if returned to Thailand. The applicant did not attend the hearing and consented to a decision on the papers, providing no further evidence. The Tribunal did not accept her claims as credible or well-founded.

Key holding: Under s 5AAA, an applicant bears the responsibility to specify all particulars of a protection claim and provide sufficient evidence to establish it; the Tribunal is not obliged to assist.

S 5AAA of the Act imposes on the applicant the responsibility of specifying all particulars of their claim to be a person to whom Australia has protection obligations, and to provide sufficient evidence to establish the claim. The Tribunal is not obliged to assist in specifying the applicant's claims or to establish or assist in establishing a claim.

entry.title: Kaur (Migration) [2024] AATA 3709
entry.content:
The applicant sought a Skilled (Provisional) (Class VC) Subclass 485 visa but was refused because she had previously been refused a student visa for failing PIC 4020(1). The Tribunal affirmed the refusal, finding PIC 4020(2) was not met and that the PIC 4020(4) waiver should not be exercised.

Key holding: Under PIC 4020(4), PIC 4020(1) and (2) may be waived only if there are compelling circumstances affecting Australia’s interests or compassionate or compelling circumstances affecting an Australian citizen, permanent resident or eligible New Zealand citizen that justify granting the visa.

The requirements of PIC 4020(1) and (2) may be waived where there are compelling circumstances that affect the interests of Australia, or where there are compassionate or compelling circumstances that affect the interests of an Australian citizen, an Australian permanent resident, or an eligible New Zealand citizen (as defined in reg 1.03), that justify the granting of the visa.

entry.title: Dumbaya (Migration) [2024] AATA 3844
entry.content:
This was a review of a delegate’s refusal of a Child (Migrant) (Class AH) visa for Mr Eddie Sheka Sidique. The Tribunal found that a purported Sierra Leone High Court order and other information supporting the visa were bogus or false, so the applicant did not meet PIC 4020(1), and it declined to waive PIC 4020. The Tribunal affirmed the refusal.

Key holding: PIC 4020(1) is engaged by a bogus document or false or misleading material information where some person has engaged in fraud or deception, even if the applicant did not know the information was untrue.

While PIC 4020 refers to information that is false, in the sense of purposely untrue, it is not necessary for the Minister (or the Tribunal on review) to conclude that the applicant was aware the information was purposely untrue in order for PIC 4020 to be engaged. However, an element of fraud or deception by some person is necessary to attract the operation of the provision: Trivedi v MIBP [2014] FCAFC 42.

Administrative Review Tribunal, 25 Sep 2024, [2024] AATA 3844

entry.title: Wang (Migration) [2024] AATA 3566
entry.content:
Ms Wang held a Subclass 010 (Bridging A) visa subject to condition 8115, which prevented her from working in Australia other than in a business visitor activity. After ABF officers located her undertaking massage work, a delegate cancelled the visa under s 116(1)(b) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Tribunal affirmed cancellation, finding the ground was made out and discretionary factors weighed in favour of cancellation.

entry.title: 2313641 (Migration) [2024] AATA 4283
entry.content:
The Tribunal affirmed cancellation of the applicant’s Subclass 500 (Student) visa after finding he gave incorrect funding information and caused a bogus fixed deposit summary to be submitted with his visa application. The Tribunal relied on the Department’s Document Examination Unit assessment and gave little weight to later bank and family-support evidence. The cancellation stood under s 109(1) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth).

Key holding: A document is a bogus document under s 5(1)(b) where the Tribunal reasonably suspects it is counterfeit, and a visa may be cancelled for providing incorrect funding information together with such a document.

It follows that the Tribunal finds that the Fixed Deposit summary from [Bank 1], [Account Number 1], Name: [Mr A] son of [Mr B] (sole owner), with principal amount of INR 2,480,000 as at 18 February 2022 and maturity amount of INR 2,606,702.00, with maturity date of 19 Feb 2023 is a bogus documents as defined in s 5(1)(b) of the Act.

entry.title: Kamboj (Migration) [2024] AATA 3382
entry.content:
Mr Kamboj sought review of a delegate’s decision to cancel his Subclass 500 (Student) visa under s 109 of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Department found he provided incorrect education information in both student visa applications and bogus education documents in the first application. The Tribunal affirmed the cancellation.

Key holding: Non-compliance under s 101(b) and s 103 is established where an applicant provides incorrect information in visa applications and causes bogus documents to be given in an earlier application.

The Tribunal therefore finds that the applicant has provided incorrect information in the first and second visa applications and caused bogus documents to be given in the first visa application. It follows that there has been non-compliance by the applicant with s 101(b) and s 103 of the Act in the way described in the s 107 notice.

Administrative Review Tribunal, 11 Sep 2024, [2024] AATA 3382

entry.title: 1800607 (Refugee) [2024] AATA 4361
entry.content:
The applicant, who claims Indonesian citizenship, sought review of a delegate’s refusal of a protection visa. The Tribunal found she had provided a fraudulently altered Indonesian passport as identity evidence and rejected her explanations for it. It affirmed the refusal because s 91WA of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) required refusal.

Key holding: Under s 91WA(1) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth), the Minister, and the Tribunal on review, must refuse to grant a protection visa if the applicant provides, or causes to be provided, a bogus document as evidence of identity, nationality or citizenship, or destroys or disposes of such documentary evidence.

Section 91WA(1) of the Act requires the Minister to refuse to grant a protection visa to an applicant who provides, or causes to be provided, a bogus document as evidence of their identity, nationality or citizenship, or if the Minister is satisfied the applicant has destroyed or disposed, or caused the destruction or disposal, of documentary evidence of their identity, nationality or citizenship.

Administrative Review Tribunal, 6 Sep 2024, [2024] AATA 4361

entry.title: 2302773 (Migration) [2024] AATA 4292
entry.content:
The Tribunal reviewed cancellation of the applicant’s Subclass 500 (Student) visa, granted as a dependent of his spouse, under s 109(1) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Department cancelled because the applicant had previously held student visas under a different name and date of birth and, in the 2021 application, failed to disclose that identity and provided a passport obtained by false or misleading information.

Key holding: A passport obtained through a false or misleading statement, including by omitting a prior passport, is a bogus document under s 5(1)(c), and causing it to be given breaches s 103.

The Tribunal therefore finds the passport in the name of [the applicant] ([DOB 1]), with number [1] is a bogus document within the meaning of s 5(1)(c) as it was obtained because of a false or misleading statement. The Tribunal is of the view the applicant has caused a bogus document to be given.

entry.title: LFFQ and Minister for Immigration and Multicultural Affairs (Migration) [2024] AATA 3429
entry.content:
LFFQ, a 54-year-old Bangladeshi citizen, sought review of a delegate’s refusal of his Bridging E visa under s 501 of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The delegate found he failed the character test because of a South Korean conviction for a sexually based offence involving a child, and the Tribunal affirmed the refusal applying Direction No 110.

Key holding: An administrative tribunal exercising migration character powers cannot contradict or go behind a criminal conviction.

The Tribunal's observation that it could not contradict or go behind a conviction was correct.

entry.title: 1829009 (Refugee) [2024] AATA 3962
entry.content:
This was an AATA review of a delegate’s refusal to grant a protection visa to a Malaysian citizen of Kadazan ethnicity and Christian faith. The applicant claimed employment discrimination, limited opportunities and poverty in Sabah; the Tribunal accepted some discrimination but found the harm did not meet the protection thresholds. It affirmed the refusal.

Key holding: Employment discrimination causing only relative economic disadvantage, without serious harm as defined in s 5J(5), does not establish a well-founded fear of persecution.

Thus, the Tribunal finds that the level of harm the applicant will experience does not rise to the level of constituting serious harm as outlined in s 5J(5) of the Act.

entry.title: 2411742 (Refugee) [2024] AATA 4375
entry.content:
The applicant is an older South Korean citizen who claimed protection in Australia because he feared being unable to find work in South Korea due to age discrimination and long absence. The Tribunal affirmed the refusal of his protection visa, finding South Korea offers effective protection against age discrimination and that his economic/employment concerns did not meet protection criteria.

Key holding: Effective protection measures available from the receiving State can negate a well-founded fear of persecution under s 5J(2).

The Tribunal finds, therefore, that South Korea can offer effective protection to its citizens against age discrimination. It follows, and the Tribunal finds, that effective protection measures against age discrimination are available to the applicant in South Korea, and that therefore he does not have a well-founded fear of persecution on that ground: s 5J(2).
